beats.say: At events, hundreds of people join one network. An attacker can set up another with the same name.
An open, strong network with a similar name may be a trap. Ask registration for the right name.
For work, use mobile data or your organisation's VPN. Never type your work password on a Wi-Fi sign-in page.
Instead of a public charging station, plug your own adapter into a socket or use your own power bank.

scenes.title: The forum Wi-Fi
scenes.intro: At the forum you joined an open network and the browser opened. Choose the right step on each page.

steps.label: ReqemYol-Forum-FREE
steps.say: What is this Wi-Fi page asking for?

actions.label: Connect to internet
actions.feedback: A Wi-Fi page never needs your work password. Whoever runs this open network now sees it.

actions.label: Close tab
actions.feedback: Correct. Leave the network and ask the registration desk for the right name.

actions.label: Leave network
actions.feedback: Excellent. Leaving an unknown open network is the fastest protection.

body.text: The certificate for poct.idare.example is not valid.
Someone may be trying to read your data.

steps.say: You open work mail and the browser shows a warning.

actions.label: Go back
actions.feedback: Correct. This warning can mean someone is in the middle of your connection, so switch to mobile data.

actions.label: Continue anyway
actions.feedback: Skipping the warning can hand your password to whoever sits in the middle. Go back and change networks.

steps.say: The page offers software for the Wi-Fi.

actions.label: Open file
actions.feedback: Joining Wi-Fi needs no software. This file installs malware on the computer.

actions.label: Delete
actions.feedback: Correct. An event network never requires you to install software.

scenes.prompt: Which networks at the event look suspicious? Find them.

spots.label: FREE added
spots.explain: The network is open and FREE was added to the name. The official name is given at the registration desk.

spots.label: Look-alike name
spots.explain: The name is almost the official one, only one character differs. This may be an evil twin.

spots.label: Tempting name
spots.explain: An open network with a free offer is a classic sign of a trap.

question.prompt: Your phone is at 5 percent and the hall has a public USB charging station. What do you do?

options.label: Plug my own adapter into a wall socket
options.feedback: Correct. A socket delivers only power, not data.

options.label: Charge from my own power bank
options.feedback: Right. Your own power bank stays under your control.

options.label: Connect to the station and tap Trust
options.feedback: Trusting gives the device access to your phone's data. Charging does not need it.

options.label: Borrow the cable of the guest next to me
options.feedback: An unknown cable can hide a chip inside. Carry your own cable and adapter.

scenes.explain: Your own adapter in a socket or your own power bank is the safest. If the phone asks, do not trust.

scenes.prompt: Things that arrive during the event. Safe, or a threat?

messages.text: Your badge is ready. Bring your ID card to the registration desk.

cards.explain: No link, nothing to pay and nothing to type. This is a normal reminder.

body.text: Sign in with your work email to download the certificate:

cards.explain: The official site is reqemyol-forum.example, and this is a different domain. A certificate never needs your work password.

caption.text: Sticker on the table: scan for free Wi-Fi

cards.explain: Anyone can put up a sticker, and the address is not the forum's. Ask the registration desk for the network name.
This comes from the app you installed from the official store. No link and no request.

body.text: The connected device wants access to your phone's files.

cards.explain: A charging station should not ask for your files. Choose Don't trust and charging carries on.

points: Ask the registration desk for the network name, and use mobile data or VPN for work.
Never type your work password on a Wi-Fi page or skip a certificate warning.
Charge with your own adapter in a socket or your own power bank.
